item.title: LabWired allows engineers to test compiled firmware on simulated MCU boards (CPU and peripherals)
item.description: Andrii Shylenko’s LabWired is an MIT-licensed MCU firmware simulation core that runs compiled firmware against modeled CPUs and peripherals, captures UART and bus output, register state, and supports repeatable checks in CI. The simulator works on Arm Cortex-M0+, Cortex-M3, Cortex-M4, Cortex-M7, Cortex-M33 cores, RISC-V architecutre, and Xtensa LX6 and LX7 (some ESP32 parts). The main benefit of the project is speeding up firmware testing since doing some on real boards is slow. The hardware must be ready, then the firmware must be flashed to the board each time you want to test it, and if something breaks, developers get a dark LED and no trace. If a firmware project needs to support multiple boards, this quickly adds up. The project is different from a CPU/MCU emulator for two main reasons: The full board is modeled, not only the chip. Sensors, displays, and bus devices are also simulated. item.title: KiCad 10 now (unofficially) runs in a web browser or Android
item.description: It’s now possible to run KiCad 10 directly in a web browser or as an Android app thanks to two separate open-source projects, unaffiliated with the official KiCad project. Let’s have a look at both. Ziro Designer/ZiroEDA – KiCad 10 in your web browser Akshay Rukade (ZiroEDA), an engineering student in India, ported KiCad 10.0.6 to the browser through the Ziro Designer/ZiroEDA Designer project. It’s a TypeScript translation of KiCad’s C++, kept file-for-file against the KiCad implementation, so the real schematic editor, PCB editor, interactive router, and ERC/DRC run in a browser tab and read and write normal KiCad projects. That means you can open local KiCad projects or designs hosted on GitHub directly in a web browser without having to install KiCad 10 itself on your computer, and it should also enable machines that do not natively support KiCad (e.g., RISC-V, Android tablet, iPad…) to run it. item.title: Procolored K13 Lite DTF printer review – Custom apparel printing with printer, curing oven, and heat press
item.description: Back in May, we wrote about the Procolored X One 3-in-1 laser engraver with UV and UV-DTF color printing, and the company contacted us a few months later for a review. But instead of having us review the laser engraver, they proposed that we test their K13 Lite DTF printer “developed for small businesses and creators producing customized apparel and merchandise”. Basically, a T-shirt printer using DTF (Direct-to-Film) technology.
